sections.overview: The leopard is a powerful cat native to Africa and Asia. It occupies a broad range of environments, from tropical forest to desert and mountains. Its flexible hunting and climbing abilities help it persist where other large cats may not.
sections.identification: Adults have a long body, short muscular legs, broad paws and a long tail. Their coats range from pale gold to ochre, with dark rosettes and smaller solid spots. Some are melanistic; their markings remain visible in suitable light. Adult size varies geographically. Published reported length ranges are 1.6–2.3 m for males and 1.7–1.9 m for females; corresponding reported masses are 31–65 kg and 17–58 kg. Males are generally larger, but the overlap and geographic variation mean size alone does not identify sex. A dependable general shoulder-height range was not found.
sections.habitat: Leopards use rainforest, woodland, savanna, scrub, rocky slopes and desert where cover and prey are available. They also occur in some human-used landscapes. Himalayan records reach about 5,200 metres, an exceptional local record rather than a typical habitat.
sections.diet: This carnivore hunts prey from small mammals and birds to larger ungulates. Its menu depends on locally available animals: a Gabon study found forest ungulates important, while research in Tanzania recorded substantial primate consumption. Leopards may also take livestock near farms.
sections.behavior: Leopards generally live alone, except when females travel with cubs or adults meet to mate. Activity varies: many studied savanna populations are mainly nocturnal, while some in Gabonese rainforest were largely active by day. Scent marks, calls and scratches signal presence.
sections.reproduction: After about three months of pregnancy, a female gives birth in a concealed den, commonly to two or three cubs. They remain hidden, then follow her and learn to hunt. Independence is gradual; reported ages vary among populations, from about one year to two years.
sections.ecology: The leopard consumes different prey in different habitats, so no single species defines its diet everywhere. It may carry a kill into a tree, making it less accessible to competitors. When wild prey is scarce, livestock may enter its diet and cause conflict with people.
sections.conservation: The IUCN SSC Cat Specialist Group’s account, citing Red List version 2024-2, classifies leopards as Vulnerable and reports an 11% contraction of extant range during 2016–2023. It identifies habitat loss, prey depletion, illegal killing and trade, retaliation, and poorly managed trophy hunting as pressures.
